analysis.one_liner: Massively expands federal help paying home heating and cooling bills for low-income households.
analysis.headline: The Heating and Cooling Relief Act, which would have raised heating and cooling aid to $40 billion a year, was referred to a Senate committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would authorize $400 billion over ten years for the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program, roughly ten times its recent funding level. It would roughly double who qualifies (households up to 250% of the poverty line, or anyone spending 3% or more of income on energy), add year-round cooling aid for heat waves, pay down past-due utility bills, and bar energy companies that receive program funds from shutting off service or charging late fees to assisted households for a year. It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on February 14, 2023 and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Low- and moderate-income households struggling with energy bills. The bill expands eligibility from about 150% of the poverty line to 250%, adds anyone whose energy bills eat 3% or more of income, lets applicants self-attest eligibility without income paperwork, adds dedicated cooling assistance for heat waves, and requires payment plans for past-due bills. It also raises pay for local program workers to at least $15 an hour and boosts weatherization funding.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-income households with high energy bills

how_it_helps.text: Authorizes $400 billion for home energy assistance for fiscal years 2024 through 2033, versus the program's prior authorization of $2 billion and annual appropriations of a few billion dollars.

Expands eligibility to households with incomes up to the greater of 250% of the poverty line or 80% of their state's median income, and to any household with a monthly energy burden of 3% or more; the bill's findings note that in 2019 only 16 percent of income-eligible households received aid.
Requires states to let applicants self-attest eligibility without submitting proof of income, citizenship, or need.

Creates dedicated cooling assistance for heat waves, usable for energy-efficient air conditioners, and requires federal heating and cooling aid to households in declared disaster or emergency areas, including extreme heat.

Bars energy suppliers that receive program funds for a household from shutting off that household's service for a year, and from charging late fees for six months before and after receiving funds, with refunds of fees already charged.

Requires assistance for past-due home energy bills (arrears) on top of regular aid, and raises the share of funds states may spend on weatherization from 15% to 25%, prioritizing repairs that replace fossil-fuel appliances with electric heating and cooling.
Requires states to adopt procedures protecting assisted households from shutoffs and certain late fees, and directs HHS and DOE to study shutoff and late-fee rates among eligible households.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, since the $400 billion authorization is not offset by any tax or spending cut in the bill. Energy suppliers would bear new conditions on the aid they handle: no shutoffs or late fees for assisted households, refunds of certain late fees, data-sharing for outreach, and offers of percentage-of-income payment plans within two years.

drawbacks.text: The $400 billion ten-year authorization is far larger than the program's current scale and is not paid for with any offsetting revenue or cuts in the bill, so it would add to federal deficits unless Congress separately funded and financed it.

The bill eliminates income, citizenship, and need documentation for applicants in favor of self-attestation, trading tighter verification for easier access; some taxpayers and program administrators would view the loss of verification as a risk to program integrity.

Quadrupling the income eligibility ceiling (150% to 250% of poverty) and adding an energy-burden test would greatly widen the pool seeking a finite appropriation, and the bill's requirement to prioritize decarbonization retrofits could shift money away from direct bill payment if funding falls short of the full authorization.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the households it targets, the benefits are direct and large: expanded eligibility, past-due bill relief, shutoff protections, and first-time robust cooling aid. The real cost question is scale and financing: $40 billion a year is roughly ten times what Congress has historically appropriated for this program, and the bill provides no offset, so its full promise depends on future appropriations. The paperwork-free eligibility is a genuine tradeoff between access and verification. On the merits it is a well-aimed safety-net expansion whose main weakness is its unbudgeted price tag.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced, and in nearly two years it never got a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Edward Markey introduced the bill on February 14, 2023 with six original cosponsors: Sens. Warren, Gillibrand, Blumenthal, Booker, Sanders, and Padilla.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day of introduction.
The action history shows no further action of any kind — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — through the end of the 118th Congress.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and bills not enacted die with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Energy suppliers are better off because the bill died: it would have conditioned program funds on shutoff bans, late-fee refunds, and payment plans for past-due customers. Low-income households gained nothing, and the utility and fossil-fuel heating industries avoided new obligations.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Energy suppliers; households got no relief

for.name: Sen. Edward J. Markey
for.role: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Heating and Cooling Relief Act and recruited six Senate cosponsors.

for.name: Sens. Elizabeth Warren, Kirsten Gillibrand, Richard Blumenthal, Cory Booker, Bernie Sanders, and Alex Padilla
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no further recorded action.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee (chaired by Sen. Bernie Sanders)
against.what_they_did: Held the bill without a hearing, markup, or vote for nearly two years; the committee took no recorded action after the February 14, 2023 referral.

sides.party_line_note: All seven Senate sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or the independent Bernie Sanders; no Republican signed on, and the Democratic-led committee never took the bill up.

industries.industry: Electric and gas utilities and home energy suppliers
industries.note: The bill would condition program funds on bans on shutting off assisted households for a year, six-month late-fee waivers with refunds, data-sharing for outreach, and offers of percentage-of-income payment plans. Its interest in avoiding these conditions runs against the households the bill protects.

industries.industry: Fossil-fuel heating (oil, propane, gas heating equipment)
industries.note: Households could still use aid to pay fossil-fuel heating bills, but the bill prioritizes weatherization and repair spending on replacing fossil-fuel appliances with electric heating and cooling and directs new grant programs to support a transition away from fossil fuels. Over time this nudges aid away from oil- and gas-heated homes.

Raising the weatherization share of funds from 15% to 25% of a vastly larger program, plus new $1 billion-a-year grants for energy-burden reduction plans, would steer billions into home repairs, efficiency retrofits, and electrification work, with preferences for unions and minority- and women-owned firms.
